newsitem.title: UK: BSKYB , BT TEAM UP ON DIGITAL SATELLITE.
newsitem.headline: BSKYB , BT TEAM UP ON DIGITAL SATELLITE.

text.p: British pay television giant BSkyB is gearing up to launch 200-channel digital satellite services within the next year.
BSkyB has recruited British Telecommunications, Midland Bank and Matsushita Electric of Japan as partners in a new consortium to supply services such as home shopping and home banking.

The partners in British Interactive Broadcasting (BIB) are to provide 265 million pounds ($433 million) to bring the retail price of decoder boxes for the services down to 200 pounds or less. The venture is expected to break even after five years.
Amstrad , Pace Micro Technology, Matsushita and Grundig /Hyundai will fulfill a one million set-top decoder box order by BSkyB.
"Interactive TV will add a new dimension to the broadcasting revolution in Britain and Sky again is at the forefront of these exciting changes," BSkyB chief executive Sam Chisholm said.
"The range of interactive services on offer and the set top box subsidy will make this very attractive to subscribers," he added in a statement on Wednesday.

BSkyB, in which Rupert Murdoch's News Corp is the largest shareholder, previously said it planned to launch digital satellite services late this year but now aims for a Spring 1998 start. Interactive services should become available later in 1998.
Confirmation of the digital launch gave BSkyB shares a shot in the arm. They had climbed 19.5p to 615p by midmorning as the stock has gained over six percent during the last three sessions.
BSkyB also said pre-tax profit for the nine months to end-March rose to 215 million pounds, up 21 percent. It now has 6.2 million subscribers in Britain and Ireland.
Digital satellite will offer viewers hundreds of channels, better picture and sound quality and TV services such as near video on demand and pay per view.
The interactive element will allow viewers to carry out banking transactions and buy goods from their favourite high street stores at the click of a button.
BSkyB and BT will each have stakes of 32.5 percent in the BIB consortium, while Midland Bank will hold 20 percent and Matsushita the remaining 15 percent.
The combination of Britain's leading pay television company with the dominant telephone company is certain to be examined closely by regulators.
BSkyB deputy managing director David Chance told Reuters that the company had spent months talking to Oftel and was confident that the telecoms watchdog would give its blessing.
Oftel said it was to look closely at how the venture intends to operate but that it was not its role to approve the deal.
British cable operator Telewest Communications, which plans to go digital later this year, was swift to voice its concerns.

"With respect to BIB, our only concern will be to ensure that a joint venture involving quasi-monopolists does not lead to anti-competitive behaviour. We are sure that the regulatory bodies will share this concern," Telewest chief executive Stephen Davidson said.
